arml-2016-individual-01.title: Primes must divide ab
arml-2016-individual-01.body:
$2016=2^5\cdot3^2\cdot7$, so each of $2,3,7$ divides $a$ or $b$, i.e. $42\mid ab$. Try the factorizations $ab=42$ with small sums:

- $a=6$, $b=7$: $6^7\cdot7^c$ already contains $2^7\cdot3^7\cdot7$ with $c=1$. Sum $14$.
- $a=7$, $b=6$: $7^6\cdot6^c$ needs $c\ge5$ (for $2^5$): sum $18$.
- $a=3$, $b=14$: needs $2^5$ from $14^c$, so $c\ge5$: sum $22$. $a=2$, $b=21$: $c=2$ suffices: sum $25$.

Any pair with $42\mid ab$ other than $\{6,7\}$ has $a+b\ge 14$ (since $a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}$ and the next smallest sums are $\{3,14\},\{2,21\}$ or $ab\ge84$), and $c\ge1$. So the minimum is $14$.

**Answer: 14**

arml-2016-individual-01.title: Bound and check
arml-2016-individual-01.body:
Since $42\mid ab$, $a+b\ge 2\sqrt{42}>12.9$, so $a+b\ge13$, with equality only for $\{a,b\}=\{6,7\}$; thus $a+b+c\ge14$. The triple $(6,7,1)$ gives $6^7\cdot7=2^7\cdot3^7\cdot7$, a multiple of $2016$.

**Answer: 14**

arml-2016-individual-02.title: Ratio of bases
arml-2016-individual-02.body:
If $A$ were the apex, the ant would stop at the midpoint of the base, enclosing half the area. So $A$ is a base angle; let $B$ be the apex ($AB=BC$). The ant stops at a point $P$ on $BC$ (the side opposite $A$: by the triangle inequality $AB<BC+CA$ and $AC<AB+BC$, so the half-perimeter is more than $AB$ and more than $AC$). Triangles $APB$ and $APC$ share the altitude from $A$, so their areas are in the ratio $PB:PC$, which is $9:1$ or $1:9$.

- Ant goes via $B$, enclosing $APB$: $PB=9$, $PC=1$, $AB=BC=10$; half perimeter $AB+BP=19$, so $AC=18$. Then $\tan A=\frac{\sqrt{10^2-9^2}}{9}=\frac{\sqrt{19}}9$.
- Ant goes via $C$, enclosing $APC$: $PB=1$, $PC=9$, $AB=BC=10$; half perimeter $AC+CP=AC+9=\frac{20+AC}2$, so $AC=2$. Then $\tan A=\frac{\sqrt{100-1}}{1}=3\sqrt{11}$.

The maximum is $3\sqrt{11}$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt{11}$**

arml-2016-individual-03.title: Pair consecutive terms
arml-2016-individual-03.body:
Pair $\lfloor\sqrt[4]{2k-1}\rfloor$ with $\lfloor\sqrt[4]{2k}\rfloor$. They are equal unless $2k$ is a perfect fourth power. Even fourth powers up to $2016$: $16,256,1296$. So the ratio is
$$\frac{\lfloor\sqrt[4]{15}\rfloor}{\lfloor\sqrt[4]{16}\rfloor}\cdot\frac{\lfloor\sqrt[4]{255}\rfloor}{\lfloor\sqrt[4]{256}\rfloor}\cdot\frac{\lfloor\sqrt[4]{1295}\rfloor}{\lfloor\sqrt[4]{1296}\rfloor}=\frac12\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac56=\frac5{16}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{5}{16}$**

arml-2016-individual-04.title: Cases on where 1 and 2 go
arml-2016-individual-04.body:
$1$ can only be followed by $2$, and $2$ only by $1$, $3$ or $4$; any number $\ge3$ can be followed by anything (since $2\cdot3=6$). So only what follows $1$ and $2$ matters.

- **$x_6=1$:** then $2$ is followed by $1$ (if $x_5=2$) — $4!$ arrangements of the rest — or $2$ is followed by $3$ or $4$: treat "23" or "24" as a block: $4!$ each. Total $3\cdot24=72$.
- **$x_5=1$, $x_6=2$:** the other four in any order: $24$.
- **$1$ not at the end and not right before a final $2$:** $1$ must be followed by $2$, which is followed by $3$ or $4$: blocks "123" or "124" plus three other numbers: $2\cdot4!=48$.

Total $72+24+48=144$.

**Answer: 144**

arml-2016-individual-04.title: Brute force check
arml-2016-individual-04.body:
Listing all $720$ permutations and testing $x_{i+1}\le2x_i$ (by computer) gives $144$.

**Answer: 144**

arml-2016-individual-05.title: Separate the primes
arml-2016-individual-05.body:
The equation says $16^A18^B24^C=1$, i.e. $2^{4A+B+3C}3^{2B+C}=1$. By unique factorization, $4A+B+3C=0$ and $2B+C=0$. So $C=-2B$ and $4A=5B$: $(A,B,C)=t(5,4,-8)$. The least nonzero value is at $t=\pm1$: $25+16+64=105$.

**Answer: 105**

arml-2016-individual-06.title: Find the right triangles, then angle-chase
arml-2016-individual-06.body:
Let $JO=x$, $SE=y$. Then $JE^2=81+y^2=x^2-400$, so $x^2-y^2=481$; with $x+y=37$, $x-y=13$, so $x=25$, $y=12$, $JE=15$.

Triangles $JSE$ ($9,12,15$) and $JEO$ ($15,20,25$) are both $3$-$4$-$5$ triangles. Let $\theta=\angle JOE$, so $\tan\theta=\frac{15}{20}=\frac34$. In $\triangle JSE$, $\tan\angle JES=\frac9{12}=\frac34$, so $\angle JES=\theta$, and $\angle LEO=\angle LEJ+\angle JEO=\theta+90^\circ$. Then $\angle L=180^\circ-(90^\circ+\theta)-\theta=90^\circ-2\theta$.

$\tan L=\cot2\theta=\frac{1-\tan^2\theta}{2\tan\theta}=\frac{7/16}{3/2}=\frac7{24}$, $\sin L=\frac7{25}$. In right triangle $LSJ$: $LS=\frac{9}{\tan L}=\frac{216}7$, $LJ=\frac9{\sin L}=\frac{225}7$, so $LS+LJ=63$.

Perimeter $=LS+SE+EO+OJ+JL=63+12+20+25=120$.

**Answer: 120**

arml-2016-individual-06.title: Similar 7-24-25 triangle
arml-2016-individual-06.body:
As above, $SE=12$, $JE=15$, $JO=25$, and $\triangle JSE\sim\triangle JEO$. With $\alpha=\angle EOJ=\angle JES$, we get $\angle L=90^\circ-2\alpha$ (angle sum in $\triangle LEO$), so in right triangle $LSJ$, $\angle LJS=2\alpha$. $\sin2\alpha=2\cdot\frac35\cdot\frac45=\frac{24}{25}$, so $\triangle LSJ$ is a $7$-$24$-$25$ triangle with the side $JS=9$ opposite $\angle L$ playing the role of $7$: scale $\frac97$, $LS=24\cdot\frac97$, $LJ=25\cdot\frac97$, sum $49\cdot\frac97=63$. Perimeter $63+37+20=120$.

**Answer: 120**

arml-2016-individual-07.title: Which side is the hypotenuse?
arml-2016-individual-07.body:
All three lengths must be positive, so $0<\cos x<1$ and $\tan x=\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}>\sin x$. So $\sin x$ is not the hypotenuse.

- **Hypotenuse $\tan x$:** $\tan^2x=\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$, $x=45^\circ$, legs $\frac{\sqrt2}2$, area $\frac14$.
- **Hypotenuse $\cos x$:** $\cos^2x=\sin^2x+\tan^2x$. Multiply by $\cos^2x$: $\cos^4x=(1-\cos^2x)\cos^2x+(1-\cos^2x)$, i.e. $2\cos^4x=1$, $\cos x=2^{-1/4}$, $\sin^2x=1-\frac{\sqrt2}2$. Area $=\frac{\sin x\tan x}2=\frac{\sin^2x}{2\cos x}=\frac{2^{1/4}}2\left(1-\frac{\sqrt2}2\right)=\frac{\sqrt[4]2}2-\frac{\sqrt[4]8}4\approx0.174$.

Compare with $\frac14$: $\frac{\sqrt[4]2}2-\frac{\sqrt[4]8}4=\frac18(4\sqrt[4]2-2\sqrt[4]8)$, and $4\sqrt[4]2<5$ (since $512<625$), $2\sqrt[4]8>3$ (since $128>81$), so it is less than $\frac18\cdot2=\frac14$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt[4]{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt[4]{8}}{4}$**

arml-2016-individual-09.title: Condition on the first two dice
arml-2016-individual-09.body:
Let the rolls be $a$ (8-sided), $b$ (12-sided), $c$ (20-sided). Given $a,b$, the triple works if $c=a+b$, $c=a-b$, or $c=b-a$ (at most two of these are possible values, never coinciding).

- $c=a+b\le20$ always possible: probability $\frac1{20}$.
- $c=|a-b|$ possible iff $a\ne b$: probability $\frac1{20}\cdot P(a\ne b)=\frac1{20}\cdot\left(1-\frac{8}{96}\right)=\frac1{20}\cdot\frac{11}{12}$.

Total $\frac1{20}+\frac{11}{240}=\frac{23}{240}$.

**Answer: $\frac{23}{240}$**

arml-2016-individual-09.title: Count triples
arml-2016-individual-09.body:
Out of $8\cdot12\cdot20=1920$ triples: $c=a+b$ holds for exactly one $c$ for each of the $96$ pairs $(a,b)$. The cases $a=b+c$ and $b=a+c$ together mean $c=|a-b|$ with $a\ne b$: one triple for each of the $96-8=88$ pairs with $a\ne b$. These cases never overlap. Total $184$, and $\frac{184}{1920}=\frac{23}{240}$.

**Answer: $\frac{23}{240}$**

arml-2016-individual-tb1.title: Sizes of permutation classes
arml-2016-individual-tb1.body:
Group solutions by their multiset $\{a,b,c,d\}$. A class has size $24$ (all distinct), $12$ (one pair), $6$ (two pairs), $4$ (three equal) or $1$ (all equal).

$43$ is odd, so some class has size $1$: $N=4m^2$. And $42\equiv2\pmod4$, while $24,12,4$ are multiples of $4$, so there must be a two-pairs class: $N=2a^2+2c^2$ with $a\ne c$, i.e. $N/2=2m^2$ is a sum of two distinct squares.

- $m=1,2,3,4$: $N/2=2,8,18,32$ — none is a sum of two distinct positive squares.
- $m=5$: $N=100$, $N/2=50=1^2+7^2$. ✓

For $N=100$: $100=5^2\cdot4$ (size 1), $1+1+49+49$ (size 6), and $81+9+9+1$, $64+16+16+4$, $49+25+25+1$ (size 12 each). There are no three-equal classes other than $5,5,5,5$ (checking $(100-d^2)/3$), and no all-distinct class (all four have the same parity since $100\equiv0\pmod4$; even ones give at least $4+16+36+64=120$, odd ones give $84$ or at least $116$).

Total $1+6+3\cdot12=43$.

**Answer: 100**

arml-2016-individual-tb1.title: Computer check
arml-2016-individual-tb1.body:
Counting ordered representations $N=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$ with positive integers for every $N\le100$ shows the count is first exactly $43$ at $N=100$.

**Answer: 100**

arml-2016-individual-tb2.title: Dissect
arml-2016-individual-tb2.body:
Split $HEXAGON$ into hexagon $HEAGON$ and $\triangle AXE$.

**$[HEAGON]$:** extend $HE$ and $ON$ to meet at $Q$, and $ON$ and $AG$ to meet at $R$. Triangles $HNQ$ and $GOR$ are isosceles right triangles with hypotenuse $8$ and legs $4\sqrt2$, each of area $16$. $AEQR$ is a rectangle with sides $QR=8+8\sqrt2$ and $QE=8+4\sqrt2$, so
$$[HEAGON]=(8+8\sqrt2)(8+4\sqrt2)-32=96+96\sqrt2.$$

**$[AXE]$:** $EA=8+8\sqrt2$ (a long diagonal parallel to two sides). By symmetry $X$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $EA$; let $Y$ be its foot on $EA$. Since $HA\parallel ET$ and $HE\parallel XY$, $\triangle XYE\sim\triangle HEA$ with ratio $\frac{EY}{EA}=\frac12$, so $XY=\frac12HE=4$. Then $[AXE]=\frac12(8+8\sqrt2)\cdot4=16+16\sqrt2$.

Total: $112+112\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $112+112\sqrt2$**

arml-2016-individual-tb2.title: Coordinates check
arml-2016-individual-tb2.body:
Place the octagon with circumradius $R=\frac{8}{2\sin22.5^\circ}$ and vertices at angles $0^\circ,45^\circ,\dots$ in the order $H,E,P,T,A,G,O,N$. Intersecting lines $ET$ and $PA$ and applying the shoelace formula to $H,E,X,A,G,O,N$ gives area $\approx270.39$, which equals $112+112\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $112+112\sqrt2$**

arml-2016-individual-tb3.title: Each term is a cube minus one
arml-2016-individual-tb3.body:
$mmm_{m+1}=m\left((m+1)^2+(m+1)+1\right)=(m+1)^3-1$ (it is the largest 3-digit number in base $m+1$). So the sum is
$$\sum_{k=2}^{9}(k^3-1)=\left(\frac{9\cdot10}2\right)^2-1-8=2025-9=2016.$$

**Answer: 2016**
